paragraphs: Attention mechanisms expose weights that offer a view into a model’s internal behavior. That visibility makes them tempting to use as explanations, but the paper asks whether inspecting those weights provides the same understanding as an explanation produced after the model makes a prediction. The distinction matters because an accessible internal signal can still give an incomplete account.

The authors investigate this question mathematically using a simple attention-based architecture. They compare attention-based explanations with post-hoc explanations and identify differences between what the two approaches reveal. Their analysis finds that the resulting explanations can differ substantially, so the methods should not be treated as interchangeable ways of describing the model.

Within this analysis, post-hoc methods can capture more useful insights than attention weights alone, despite having limitations themselves. The contribution is a mathematical clarification of the debate over attention as explanation. It supports looking beyond attention weights when interpreting the studied architecture, while keeping the conclusion tied to the simple setting the authors analyze.
icml-2024-attention-meets-post-hoc-inter.tldr: A mathematical analysis of a simple attention architecture shows that post-hoc explanations can reveal more useful insights than attention weights alone.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether weaker vision-language models can help a stronger model generalize. Its starting point is that improving a single model through increasingly elaborate fine-tuning methods has delivered limited advances. The authors find that combining pretrained models offers another route: models with weaker individual performance can still improve the generalization of a strong model.

They develop three ensemble strategies matched to different information and computing conditions. When only pretrained models are available, a zero-shot ensemble automatically adjusts their prediction scores according to confidence. This gives the combination a way to account for how confident its members are, rather than relying only on which model is strongest overall.

When a few labeled examples are available, the paper offers both a training-free ensemble and a tuning-based ensemble. These alternatives accommodate different computing resources. The central finding is that individual model strength does not fully determine usefulness within a group: the tested weaker models can contribute to better generalization when combined through a strategy suited to the available resources.
icml-2024-beyond-sole-strength-customize.tldr: Customized ensembles allow weaker pretrained vision-language models to improve a stronger model’s generalization under different data and computing conditions.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series together should create opportunities to use relationships between them. Yet the paper starts from an empirical puzzle: recent models that handle each series individually frequently outperform multivariate models. CATS addresses how those relationships are represented and supplied to a forecasting model, rather than assuming that joint modeling automatically makes them useful.

The method constructs auxiliary time series from the original observations. These derived series serve as additional inputs that represent relationships across the original series. The construction behaves like an attention mechanism spanning time and context. Separate modules implement three principles the authors identify for useful auxiliary series: continuity, sparsity, and variability.

With this construction, even a basic predictor consisting of a two-layer multilayer perceptron achieves reported state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The authors also report substantially lower complexity and fewer parameters than previous multivariate models. The result points to the value of organizing cross-series information before prediction: a comparatively simple predictor can perform strongly when auxiliary inputs make those relationships more usable.
icml-2024-cats-enhancing-multivariate-ti.tldr: CATS constructs auxiliary time series that help a simple predictor exploit relationships between series while reducing model complexity.

paragraphs: CauDiTS tackles classification when labeled multivariate time series come from one domain but the model must operate in another domain without labels. Differences between the domains can make learned relationships unreliable. The paper argues that directly extracting shared features overlooks underlying causal patterns, especially when several variables interact within a complex dynamic system.

Its adaptive rationale disentangler separates relationships into domain-common causal rationales and domain-specific correlations. The intended benefit is to retain stable reasons for a classification while filtering changes specific to a domain. Stability across domains is central to this approach: it supplies the basis for learning representations that can transfer despite distribution differences.

The framework also encourages examples from the same class to have consistent causal rationales across domains. It does this through causal prototype consistency and domain-intervention causality invariance. Evaluations on four benchmark datasets report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the framework’s usefulness for the tested adaptation tasks, where the challenge is transferring classification ability without obtaining labels in the target domain.
icml-2024-caudits-causal-disentangled-do.tldr: CauDiTS improves time-series domain adaptation by separating shared causal rationales from domain-specific correlations.

paragraphs: DiNADO improves a method for steering language generation called NADO. The original approach aims to preserve existing model abilities while converging, with sufficient modeling capacity, to an optimal solution that maximizes entropy. Its practical implementation nevertheless faces several obstacles: weak gradients for low-probability control signals, dependence on regularization, and limited capacity from a small number of added transformer layers.

The proposed change separates the step-wise global normalization from the approximate oracle values assigned to possible next tokens. This reformulation allows DiNADO to work with fine-tuning methods such as LoRA. That compatibility matters because it expands the adaptation options beyond the extra-layer implementation whose capacity the authors identify as restrictive.

The paper presents theoretical and empirical arguments for improvements in capacity, stability, and flexibility. Experiments examine formality control in machine translation and lexically constrained generation on CommonGen, with reported improvements in both settings. The contribution is therefore a reformulation of an existing control approach that makes it more adaptable to different training methods and more effective on the evaluated generation tasks.
icml-2024-dinado-norm-disentangled-neura.tldr: DiNADO reformulates NADO’s normalization to improve controllable generation and enable integration with fine-tuning methods such as LoRA.

paragraphs: Diffusion models have been less successful on discrete data such as language than on many other generation tasks. The paper attributes a key difficulty to extending score matching, the theory underlying standard diffusion training, to discrete structures. It introduces score entropy, a loss designed to bring that training principle into discrete spaces by estimating distribution ratios.

The resulting Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion models, or SEDD, are evaluated on language modeling. At comparable model sizes, the authors report perplexity reductions of 25–75% against existing language diffusion approaches and competitive performance with autoregressive models, including improvements over GPT-2. They also report roughly 6–8 times better generative perplexity than GPT-2 when neither uses distribution annealing.

SEDD additionally supports a tradeoff between computation and generation quality, with a reported setting achieving similar quality using 32 times fewer network evaluations. Its controllable infilling supports generation arrangements beyond left-to-right prompting and matches nucleus sampling quality in the reported comparison. These findings make the contribution both a discrete diffusion training objective and a demonstration of more flexible language generation.
icml-2024-discrete-diffusion-modeling-by.tldr: SEDD uses a new discrete score-matching loss to improve language diffusion performance while supporting flexible infilling and compute–quality tradeoffs.

paragraphs: The paper examines a concealed route by which copyrighted material can influence a latent diffusion model. Conventional visual auditing looks for copyrighted samples included directly in training data. The authors argue that this approach overlooks training examples that look very different from a copyrighted original but can induce the effect of training on that original.

These examples are described as disguises. They require indirect access to the copyrighted material, yet their appearance does not reveal the connection through visual inspection. The important distinction is between what a training sample looks like and the effect it has on the model. A dataset can therefore evade the visual checks considered in the paper while retaining this concealed influence.

The work investigates how such disguises are generated, how their concealed connection can be revealed, and how they can be detected to supplement existing auditing tools. It also introduces a broader notion of acknowledgment for reasoning about indirect access. The contribution expands the technical scope of auditing beyond direct visual resemblance and identifies a specific mechanism that those audits need to address.
icml-2024-disguised-copyright-infringeme.tldr: Visually dissimilar training samples can conceal the influence of copyrighted originals, motivating additional detection methods for latent diffusion models.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network often involves identifying a smaller subgraph that helps account for its prediction. Searching for that subgraph can be expensive, and the way it is constructed affects which explanations are possible. This paper argues that selecting nodes can produce unintuitive disconnected nodes or miss important structures that a different construction would capture.

EiG-Search instead constructs explanations through selected edges. The authors find this approach more comprehensive than other subgraph-inducing techniques. They also emphasize choosing the explanation size separately for each instance, because different graphs can depend on important structures of different sizes. This avoids making a single explanation size the organizing principle for every prediction.

The method requires no explainer training. It ranks edges using an enhanced gradient-based importance measure and searches the edge-induced subgraphs in linear time. Experiments across seven datasets report stronger performance and efficiency than leading baselines, supported by quantitative and qualitative comparisons. The contribution combines a broader choice of explanatory structures with an efficient way to search for them.
icml-2024-eig-search-generating-edge-ind.tldr: EiG-Search produces instance-specific graph explanations through a training-free, linear-time search over edge-induced subgraphs.

paragraphs: FiT addresses a difficulty in diffusion-based image generation: models can struggle when asked to produce resolutions outside those encountered during training. A fixed image shape also constrains how diverse aspect ratios are handled. The paper proposes a transformer architecture intended to generate images across unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios.

Its central change is to represent images as dynamically sized token sequences rather than fixed-resolution grids. This supports a training strategy that accommodates different aspect ratios during both learning and generation. The authors connect that flexibility to better resolution generalization and to eliminating biases introduced by cropping images to fit a prescribed shape.

The design also includes changes to the network structure and extrapolation techniques that require no additional training. Experiments report strong performance across a broad range of resolutions. Together, these results support treating image size as a flexible part of the representation and training process. The stated goal is unrestricted generation, while the reported evidence concerns performance across the resolutions evaluated in the experiments.
icml-2024-fit-flexible-vision-transforme.tldr: FiT uses flexible token sequences and training-free extrapolation techniques to improve diffusion image generation across resolutions and aspect ratios.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find approximate stationary points of non-convex losses while maintaining differential privacy. Such points have small gradients, making them a target for optimization in settings where finding a global minimum is difficult. The authors propose a flexible framework that combines two private optimization procedures rather than designing every solver independently.

The first procedure approximately minimizes risk and supplies a warm start to a second private algorithm that searches for stationary points. This framework yields improved rates for smooth non-convex empirical losses and optimal rates for quasar-convex functions and functions satisfying the Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz condition. Those structural conditions matter: the optimality claims are attached to the specified function classes.

The authors also obtain improved rates for non-convex population losses and generalized linear models. With a modification, the approach achieves nearly the same rates for second-order stationary points when the Hessian is Lipschitz. Across these results, the contribution is a reusable way to improve private optimization guarantees, with the precise strength of each guarantee depending on the loss and its mathematical properties.
icml-2024-how-to-make-the-gradients-smal.tldr: Warm-starting private stationarity algorithms with private risk minimizers improves optimization rates and achieves optimal rates for specified function classes.

paragraphs: HumanTOMATO tackles generating coordinated facial expressions, hand gestures, and body movement from a text description. The task aims for motions that are diverse, high quality, and coherent across the whole body. The paper identifies two shortcomings in earlier work: insufficient attention to fine hand and face control, and weak alignment between generated movement and the text.

The framework includes a hierarchical motion representation and generator. A Holistic Hierarchical VQ-VAE and a Hierarchical-GPT use two structured codebooks for detailed body and hand motion reconstruction and generation. This design provides an organized representation for those motion components, addressing the need for detail within a broader whole-body generation task.

A separate pretrained text-motion alignment model explicitly helps the generated movement match the description. The approach therefore addresses both how motion is represented and how its meaning connects to language. The reported experiments show significant advantages in motion quality and text alignment. These findings support the combined design for producing expressive whole-body movement that follows the supplied description.
icml-2024-humantomato-text-aligned-whole.tldr: HumanTOMATO combines hierarchical motion modeling with explicit text-motion alignment to improve text-driven whole-body generation.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses the training information in a large dataset into a smaller collection of synthetic examples. The paper addresses the difficulty of extending successful small-dataset methods to larger, higher-resolution datasets and larger neural architectures. Its proposed algorithm, D3S, approaches that scaling problem by treating distillation as a domain-shift problem.

This reframing supplies a mathematical target: the authors derive a universal bound on distillation loss and develop an efficient method for approximately optimizing it. The distinction between the bound and its approximate optimization matters. The approach provides a principled objective together with a practical way to pursue it at scales that earlier distillation methods struggled to handle.

D3S reports state-of-the-art results on Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, and ImageNet-21K against a variety of recent baselines, including strong transfer across architectures. Ablation studies also show that validation-time hyperparameters materially affect distillation performance. That finding motivates standardized evaluation choices, because apparent differences between distillation methods can depend on how the resulting synthetic datasets are assessed.
icml-2024-large-scale-dataset-distillati.tldr: D3S reframes dataset distillation as domain shift to scale synthetic-data compression and improve transfer across neural architectures.

paragraphs: This paper proposes that neural noise can help create perceptual grouping and image segmentation. Instead of treating noise solely as interference, the authors investigate whether it can supply information for separating objects. They mathematically show that this is possible under assumptions they describe as realistic, making the claim conditional on the setting of their analysis.

They also demonstrate that adding noise to a deep neural network enables image segmentation without training on segmentation labels. To examine how closely this behavior resembles human grouping, they introduce six Good Gestalt datasets. The models reproduce several perceptual phenomena, including illusory contours, closure, continuity, proximity, and occlusion, and the authors describe the approach as sample-efficient.

On the Good Gestalt datasets, the model improves segmentation performance by a reported 24.9% compared with the other unsupervised models tested. These results support noise as a useful ingredient in unsupervised segmentation and suggest a possible explanation for perceptual grouping. The proposed connection to human perception is an interpretation supported by the observed grouping behaviors, rather than a definitive account of how human vision works.
icml-2024-latent-noise-segmentation-how-.tldr: Neural noise can enable segmentation without segmentation labels and reproduce several human perceptual grouping phenomena.

paragraphs: NeWRF aims to reduce the measurement work needed to understand wireless coverage at a site. Conventional site surveys require an experienced engineer to collect extensive channel measurements. The paper instead trains a neural model from a sparse set of measurements and uses it to predict wireless channels at locations that have not been visited.

The framework builds on Neural Radiance Fields, an approach originally associated with modeling light. Transferring that idea to wireless prediction requires accounting for differences between optical and wireless propagation. NeWRF introduces techniques that incorporate wireless propagation properties into the framework, making those physical differences part of the model design.

The authors report that extensive evaluations show accurate channel prediction at unmeasured locations with substantially lower measurement density than prior state-of-the-art approaches. This makes the main practical contribution a reduction in the observations needed to reconstruct a site’s wireless field. The results support the potential to make site assessment less costly while retaining useful predictions for locations beyond the measurement set.
icml-2024-newrf-a-deep-learning-framewor.tldr: NeWRF adapts neural field modeling to wireless propagation, predicting unmeasured channels from sparse site measurements.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether large language models can be given meaningful mathematical guarantees about performance beyond their training data. The authors present what they describe as the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for pretrained LLMs. A non-vacuous bound supplies informative control over generalization, supporting the conclusion that these models can capture regularities that extend to unseen data.

Their analysis uses compression and prediction smoothing to obtain a bound valid for unbounded log-likelihood loss. They extend it to subsampling, making bound computation 900 times faster on massive datasets. To reach the compression needed for informative bounds, they introduce SubLoRA, a low-dimensional nonlinear parameterization that supports results for models with up to 849 million parameters.

The bounds also provide a way to compare the studied models. The authors find that larger models are more compressible and have better generalization bounds than smaller ones. This links a theoretical guarantee to an observed scaling pattern in their analysis. The contribution establishes meaningful evidence of generalization through compression, without requiring parameter count alone to determine how well a model can generalize.
icml-2024-non-vacuous-generalization-bou.tldr: Compression-based bounds provide informative generalization guarantees for pretrained language models with up to 849 million parameters.

paragraphs: Contrastive Distribution Methods, or CDM, address the challenge of judging open-domain generated text automatically. The approach starts with two probability distributions, one known to be better than the other, and maps their differences into quality measures. The paper draws on the relationship between increased language-model size and improved performance to motivate this source of evaluative information.

The authors develop two versions. Generative CDM uses the contrast between two language models to produce synthetic examples for training discriminator-based evaluation metrics. Discriminative CDM uses the differences between the models’ distributions directly as an evaluation signal. Both rely on a quality contrast, but they turn it into a metric through different routes.

Experiments assess coherence in multi-turn dialogue and commonsense in controllable generation. In these settings, CDM correlates more strongly with human judgments than existing automatic metrics. The findings support the usefulness of distribution comparisons for evaluating text across the tested tasks. The premise that one distribution is superior is central: it gives the contrast a direction that can be associated with quality.
icml-2024-open-domain-text-evaluation-vi.tldr: CDM turns differences between stronger and weaker language-model distributions into text-quality measures that better match human judgments on the tested tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much auxiliary public data can improve training under differential privacy when a specified amount of public data is available. It considers both local and central privacy models, with pure and approximate privacy guarantees. The focus is the best possible worst-case error for mean estimation, empirical risk minimization, and stochastic convex optimization.

The authors prove matching lower and upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. They show that these rates can be reached either by training only on public data or by treating public data as private and applying an optimal private algorithm. This result characterizes the asymptotic possibilities; it does not mean those simple approaches have the best numerical performance in every setting.

The paper then develops algorithms with better constants than those asymptotically optimal approaches. For local private mean estimation, the proposed algorithm is optimal even including constants. Experiments also report benefits over state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical and practical results together distinguish the best rate of improvement from the additional gains available through more careful use of public data.
icml-2024-optimal-differentially-private.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal private-learning error rates with public data and develops algorithms that improve constants and empirical performance.

paragraphs: OxyGenerator reconstructs global ocean deoxygenation from 1920 to 2023 using deep learning. The challenge is that historical oxygen measurements are extremely sparse because collecting them is expensive. The paper also argues that existing expert-driven numerical simulations struggle to capture dynamic changes associated with global warming and human activity, motivating a data-driven reconstruction approach.

The model uses graph message passing that varies by zone to represent oceanographic relationships across different places and times. This connects sparse observations with locations or periods where values are missing, while accommodating heterogeneity across the ocean. The authors also incorporate prior knowledge about dissolved oxygen variation and chemical effects to help calibrate uncertainty.

Against in-situ dissolved oxygen observations, OxyGenerator reduces mean absolute percentage error by a reported 38.77% relative to CMIP6 numerical simulations. This supports its reconstruction accuracy in the reported comparison. The broader contribution is a way to combine sparse observations, spatial and temporal relationships, and domain knowledge to study long-term oxygen loss, with promising potential for understanding changes in marine environments.
icml-2024-oxygenerator-reconstructing-gl.tldr: OxyGenerator combines graph learning and oceanographic knowledge to reconstruct historical oxygen loss more accurately than CMIP6 in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that decentralized training needs more attention to robustness as it becomes a way to share the computing demands of large models. Its concern is that distributing training also introduces threats that have received insufficient discussion. The authors organize their contribution around identifying those threats, describing countermeasures, and examining a concrete attack.

The attack targets pipeline-based decentralized training and can be carried out by malicious stages. The authors describe it as easy to execute and demonstrate its severity. This gives the position a specific technical basis: a participating stage can threaten the training process, so robustness needs to be addressed within the training infrastructure itself.

To respond, the paper proposes a robust framework combining a detection strategy described as providing 100% detection with mechanisms intended to keep training efficient. It demonstrates the framework’s effectiveness against the proposed threat. The stated detection result belongs to this attack-and-defense setting; the broader contribution is an argument for treating robustness as a central design issue and a proposed feasible response.
icml-2024-position-exploring-the-robustn.tldr: A poisoning attack on decentralized pipeline training motivates a robust framework combining attack detection with efficient training mechanisms.

paragraphs: Graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search finds nearby items in high-dimensional spaces by navigating connections between stored items. The paper focuses on routing decisions made when examining a node’s neighbors. Existing optimizations often rely on heuristics, so the authors formulate routing probabilistically to provide a guarantee for how neighbors are explored.

They first develop two baseline strategies using locality-sensitive techniques, then introduce PEOs. PEOs efficiently identifies which neighboring nodes should receive an exact distance calculation. The approach targets the work performed during navigation: selecting promising candidates before spending computation on precise distance evaluations can make an existing graph index more efficient.

Experiments report that adding PEOs to HNSW increases throughput by a factor of 1.6 to 2.5. The method also outperforms the leading routing technique in efficiency by 1.1 to 1.4 times in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines a probabilistic formulation with practical routing improvements, showing that decisions within graph traversal can deliver substantial speed gains without replacing the underlying index.
icml-2024-probabilistic-routing-for-grap.tldr: PEOs improves graph-based nearest-neighbor search by probabilistically selecting neighbors for exact distance computation, increasing HNSW throughput in experiments.

paragraphs: Generative models can propose new drug molecules, but moving those proposals toward experiments is difficult when practical synthesis has not been considered. This paper develops a framework for generating chemical structures while ensuring synthetic accessibility. Its central idea is to represent molecules through synthesis pathways, making how a molecule can be built part of the representation.

The authors introduce a postfix notation for those pathways and train a transformer to translate molecular graphs into that notation. This connects a proposed structure to a synthesis-based description. The framework therefore provides a route from searching molecular structures to searching structures that belong to a synthesizable chemical space.

The paper highlights three capabilities: more accurate bottom-up synthesis planning, producing structurally similar synthesizable alternatives to unsynthesizable generated molecules while preserving their properties, and exploring synthesizable structures near hit molecules. These capabilities address different stages of molecular discovery. Together, they support using synthesis-aware representations to retain useful aspects of proposed compounds while connecting molecular generation more directly to practical accessibility.
icml-2024-projecting-molecules-into-synt.tldr: A transformer translates molecular graphs into synthesis-pathway representations to generate accessible molecules and synthesizable analogs of proposed compounds.

paragraphs: This paper questions how well Transformers suit decision-making when the environment is only partially observable. In a partially observable Markov decision process, the agent’s immediate observation does not fully reveal its situation. The authors examine whether a popular sequence architecture has the structural properties needed to learn effectively in this setting.

Their theoretical argument shows that regular-language problems, which Transformers struggle to model, can be reduced to these decision problems. This connects a known modeling difficulty to partially observable reinforcement learning. The authors identify the absence of inherent recurrence as a challenge for learning the relevant inductive biases, contrasting Transformers with recurrent models.

They propose adding a point-wise recurrent structure and identify the Deep Linear Recurrent Unit as a suitable alternative. Empirical results show suboptimal Transformer performance and considerable strength for this recurrent approach in the evaluated settings. The paper thus combines a theoretical warning with experimental evidence for revisiting architecture choices, rather than treating general sequence-modeling popularity as sufficient evidence of suitability for partially observable control.
icml-2024-rethinking-transformers-in-sol.tldr: Theoretical and empirical results expose Transformer difficulties in partially observable reinforcement learning and support a recurrent alternative.

paragraphs: This paper studies how mixture-of-experts language models should be configured as model size and training resources increase. These models offer a way to reduce computation, but the authors argue that earlier scaling analyses contain arbitrary assumptions. They focus on expert size as an additional design choice that needs to be included when comparing training configurations.

The paper introduces granularity, a hyperparameter that controls the size of experts. Its scaling laws jointly account for granularity, the number of training tokens, and model size. Using these relationships, the authors derive an optimal training configuration for a given computation budget, making expert size part of the resource-allocation decision.

The analysis also finds that the efficiency gap between dense models and mixture-of-experts models grows as model size and training budget increase, in contrast to previous work. This makes granularity relevant to predictions about large-scale efficiency, as well as to choosing an individual configuration. The contribution is a scaling framework in which expert size can be adjusted alongside other training variables.
icml-2024-scaling-laws-for-fine-grained-.tldr: Scaling laws that include expert granularity identify budget-optimal MoE configurations and show a growing efficiency advantage over dense models.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the size of a language model by removing weights, but the resulting sparse model can lose performance. SPP addresses how to fine-tune such models efficiently while retaining the sparsity already created. The goal is to improve a pruned model without disrupting the structure that makes the model sparse.

The method introduces lightweight trainable row and column matrices that modify sparse weights through element-wise multiplication and residual addition. Its construction preserves both the locations of sparse weights and the overall sparsity ratio during training and when the learned changes are merged into the model. Preservation during merging matters because the final model must retain the intended sparse structure too.

Evaluations apply SPP to LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models combined with recent post-training pruning methods. The authors report significant performance gains for both unstructured and N:M sparsity, with particularly strong benefits at high sparsity levels such as 75%. These findings support parameter-efficient adaptation as a way to improve sparse models while keeping their pruning pattern intact.
icml-2024-spp-sparsity-preserved-paramet.tldr: SPP improves pruned language models through lightweight fine-tuning that preserves their sparsity pattern and ratio during training and merging.

paragraphs: WebLINX studies conversational web navigation, where an agent controls a browser while following instructions across multiple dialogue turns. The benchmark contains 100,000 interactions from 2,300 expert demonstrations on more than 150 real websites. It supplies examples for training and evaluating agents across varied navigation patterns and tasks.

Because complete web pages contain too much information for real-time language-model processing, the authors introduce a retrieval-inspired method that ranks and selects relevant HTML elements. They combine those elements with screenshots and action history to evaluate how well different models reproduce human navigation behavior. The comparison includes small text-only models and proprietary multimodal systems.

Smaller fine-tuned decoders outperform the best zero-shot models tested, including GPT-4V, and larger fine-tuned multimodal models pretrained on screenshots. However, all the fine-tuned models struggle on unseen websites. The findings distinguish strong performance in the evaluated demonstrations from transfer to unfamiliar sites, identifying generalization as a continuing challenge for conversational browser agents.
icml-2024-weblinx-real-world-website-nav.tldr: WebLINX benchmarks conversational browser agents and finds that small fine-tuned models perform strongly, while unseen websites remain difficult.
